name: Extended water fasting

angle.text: Forum users discuss 2 to 7 day water fasts for quick fat loss before a cut or lean bulk. Research on prolonged fasts shows early weight loss that includes water and lean tissue, and appearance outcomes are not studied.

summary: Multi-day water-only fasts for fast scale loss; much early loss is lean tissue and refeeding carries documented risks.
note: Refeeding syndrome and electrolyte disturbances are documented risks.
currentQuick:
An extended water fast means eating nothing and drinking only water for several days. It is discussed in forums as a shortcut to leanness.
Weight loss is quick at first, but about two-thirds of early loss is reported as lean tissue, and there are no trials on appearance outcomes.
How it works: The body first makes glucose from protein and stores, then shifts to ketosis, using ketones as fuel while minerals such as sodium and potassium fall.
Risks and caveats: Documented risks include electrolyte imbalance, gallstones and refeeding syndrome after about 4 to 5 days or more without food, which can be potentially fatal.
deepLead:
Extended or prolonged water fasting means consuming no food, only water, for more than 24 hours, typically five to twenty days in the literature. In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed for rapid fat loss before a cut or lean bulk, and for 2 to 7 day attempts.
Medical literature describes weight loss of about 0.9 kg per day in the first week, much of it early on from lean tissue and water, and documents risks including refeeding syndrome, electrolyte imbalance and gallstones.

name: 5:2 diet / alternate-day fasting

angle.text: Users follow 5:2 or alternate-day fasting to build a weekly calorie deficit and lean out. Trials show weight loss comparable to ordinary dieting, and appearance outcomes themselves are not studied.

summary: Two very low-calorie days a week, or every other day: weight loss comparable in scope to ordinary dieting, with limited evidence it does better.
note: Not recommended for pregnancy, adolescents, or people with eating disorders.
currentQuick:
The 5:2 diet restricts intake to roughly 500 to 600 calories on two non-consecutive days a week; alternate-day fasting alternates fast and normal days. Both are forms of intermittent fasting.
Studies report modest weight loss, and evidence that they beat continuous calorie restriction is limited.
How it works: Weekly calorie intake falls because of the low days; fat and some lean mass are lost, and reviews propose exercise to help retain lean mass.
Risks and caveats: Hunger, irritability, dizziness and headaches are common early. Health bodies say it is not recommended for pregnancy, children, older adults, underweight people or those with eating disorders.
deepLead:
The 5:2 diet and alternate-day fasting are two forms of intermittent energy restriction. The 5:2 pattern has two non-consecutive days of roughly 500 to 600 calories and normal eating on the other five; alternate-day fasting alternates a very low-calorie day (under about 25 percent of usual needs) with a normal "feast" day, and a modified version allows up to 25 percent of calories on fast days.
Documented in a 2011 article by Harvie and colleagues, the 5:2 diet was popularized in the UK and Australia by Michael Mosley through the 2012 BBC Horizon documentary Eat, Fast and Live Longer. Reviews report weight loss of about 2.5 to 9.9 percent in most human studies, with limited evidence that it outperforms continuous calorie restriction.

name: Keto diet

chain: Appetite drops and water is shed
angle.text: Users adopt keto to lose fat and look leaner, and some also pursue it for skin and hormone benefits. Trials show short-term weight loss with little edge over other diets once calories are matched.

summary: A very low-carb, high-fat diet used for fat loss; trials show short-term loss but little edge over other diets once calories are matched.
note: Evidence for appearance is indirect; guidance bodies do not endorse it for heart health.
currentQuick:
The keto diet limits carbohydrate so heavily that the body produces ketones from fat. It began as an epilepsy treatment in the 1920s and became a popular weight-loss diet.
In looksmaxxing circles it is used for leaning out. Reviews find short-term loss greater than low-fat diets, with the gap shrinking over time.
How it works: With carbohydrate restricted, the liver produces ketone bodies that substitute for glucose. Researchers attribute most weight loss to reduced calorie intake and adherence rather than ketosis itself.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include constipation, headache, cramps, raised LDL cholesterol and, in children on the medical diet, kidney stones and slowed growth. Rare ketoacidosis cases exist. The American Heart Association says evidence is insufficient to support it for heart health.
deepLead:
The ketogenic (keto) diet is a very low-carbohydrate, high-fat, adequate-protein eating pattern that shifts the body toward burning fat and producing ketone bodies. It originated as a medical therapy for drug-resistant epilepsy, mainly in children, and has since become a mainstream weight-loss diet. 
In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a way to lose body fat quickly and look leaner for facial and physique appearance, and members post before-and-after photos and weight-loss reports. 
Reviews describe the weight-loss evidence as mixed: low-carbohydrate diets can produce more loss than low-fat diets in the short term, but higher-quality meta-analyses find little or no difference over longer periods, and researchers attribute most loss to calorie restriction and adherence. Professional bodies such as the American Heart Association have said evidence is insufficient to support the diet for heart health.

name: Lion diet

angle.text: Followers of the lion diet eat only ruminant meat, salt and water as a stricter carnivore diet, citing leaner bodies and clearer skin. No trials exist on it, and the appearance benefits rest on anecdote.

summary: Beef, salt and water only: a carnivore-diet variant with no trials behind it and dietitian warnings about nutrient gaps.
note: No clinical studies of the lion diet itself were found.
currentQuick:
The lion diet allows only ruminant meat such as beef, plus salt and water. It is a stricter version of the carnivore diet.
It spread through social media after public figures said they followed it, and is usually discussed as an elimination approach rather than for appearance specifically.
How it works: Proponents describe it as removing all plant foods and other potential triggers. Researchers have not tested this mechanism in the lion diet.
Risks and caveats: Dietetic bodies call the carnivore diet a fad and cite raised LDL cholesterol, low fibre and vitamin deficiencies from excluding plant foods. No clinical trials of the lion diet were found.
deepLead:
The lion diet is a restrictive elimination diet consisting only of ruminant meat (typically beef), salt and water. It is described as a stricter form of the carnivore diet, which allows animal products such as meat, dairy and eggs. 
It gained wider attention after Mikhaila Peterson and her father Jordan Peterson said they followed it, and it later circulated on social media such as TikTok. 
Dietetic organisations such as the British Dietetic Association and Dietitians Australia have dismissed the carnivore diet as a fad, and commentators note concerns about nutrient gaps. No clinical trials of the lion diet itself have been found.

name: Carb cycling / refeeds

chain: Alternate high and low carb days
angle.text: Users alternate higher and lower carbohydrate days, with refeeds around training, to lean out while keeping gym performance. Direct evidence is thin, and fat loss in studies tracks total calories.

summary: Alternating high- and low-carb days to lean out; direct evidence is thin and fat loss tracks total calories.
note: Source base is a single AI-generated encyclopedia page; treat details cautiously.
currentQuick:
Carb cycling swaps higher- and lower-carbohydrate days, with high days called refeeds. It comes from bodybuilding and flexible dieting.
Believers say it keeps muscle and eases dieting. Direct research is limited.
How it works: Higher-carb days are proposed to restore glycogen, hunger hormones and training performance. Overall calorie deficit is described as the main driver of fat loss.
Risks and caveats: Possible fatigue in low-carb phases, overeating on high-carb days, and disordered eating in some people.
deepLead:
Carb cycling alternates higher-carbohydrate and lower-carbohydrate days, often around training, with higher-carbohydrate days sometimes called refeeds. Protein is usually kept roughly constant while fat is adjusted in the opposite direction to carbohydrate. 
Proponents say it preserves muscle during fat loss and helps adherence. The same source notes that direct research on carb cycling is limited, and that fat loss mainly tracks overall calorie deficit.

name: Volume eating

angle.text: Users build meals around vegetables, fruit and other bulky low-calorie foods to stay full while cutting. Energy density is a studied factor in dieting, though volume eating itself has not been studied as a looksmaxxing method.

summary: Filling meals with low-calorie-density foods to stay full on fewer calories; plausible for dieting but unstudied as a looksmaxxing method.
note: The term also describes post-surgery overeating and a compulsive-eating pattern in medical papers.
currentQuick:
Volume eating means choosing foods that give lots of bulk for few calories, such as vegetables and fruit, to feel full while dieting.
It is discussed in fat-loss circles. Source material specific to it is limited.
How it works: Low-energy-density foods supply fewer calories relative to volume, so a reduced-calorie diet built from them is described as beneficial for weight management.
Risks and caveats: No direct harms reported for the dieting strategy in the sources. The same term describes compulsive large-volume eating in psychiatric and bariatric papers.
deepLead:
Volume eating is the practice of building meals around low-energy-density foods, such as vegetables and fruit, that supply a lot of food by weight or volume for relatively few calories, with the aim of feeling full while cutting calorie intake. 
In looksmaxxing it is discussed as a way to lose body fat. Public health sources note that because fruits and vegetables have few calories relative to volume, eating them as part of a reduced-calorie diet can be beneficial for weight management.  Sources on the practice are limited, and no studies found tested it for appearance outcomes.

name: Avoiding ultra-processed foods

angle.text: Users cut ultra-processed foods to lose fat and, in some circles, to improve skin. UPF intake is linked to health outcomes in observational studies, and appearance trials of avoiding them have not been done.

summary: A whole-food approach built on the NOVA scheme; linked to health outcomes in observational studies but no appearance trials.
note: The UPF category is contested by some nutrition researchers.
currentQuick:
This approach means cutting industrially manufactured, multi-ingredient foods and eating mostly whole or minimally processed ones, often to reduce body fat.
Observational studies link UPFs to obesity and disease, but the category itself is debated.
How it works: NOVA classifies foods by processing rather than nutrients. Mechanisms linking UPFs to harm are described as unclear.
Risks and caveats: Little direct risk reported. One study noted that avoiding UPFs could change nutrient intake, since fortified breads and cereals are often classed as UPFs.
deepLead:
Avoiding ultra-processed foods (UPFs) is a whole-food dietary approach, sometimes used by people trying to lose fat, based on the NOVA food classification, in which UPFs are industrially manufactured products made from many ingredients, often including additives and ingredients rarely used in home cooking. 
Observational studies link high UPF intake with obesity and chronic disease, while critics say the category is poorly defined and that randomised evidence is limited.

name: Cotton ball diet

angle.text: The cotton ball diet is a fad in which people swallow cotton balls to feel full and eat less, aiming for a thinner look. It is untested in trials, and health experts have condemned it.

summary: Swallowing cotton balls to feel full; condemned by health experts for blockage risk.
note: Documented risk of intestinal blockage requiring surgery.
currentQuick:
The cotton ball diet involves swallowing cotton balls, often dipped in juice, in place of food to feel full.
It was reported as an online fad around 2013 and has been condemned by health professionals.
How it works: The balls are meant to fill the stomach with a non-caloric bulk. Cotton is not digestible.
Risks and caveats: Reported risks include bezoars and intestinal obstruction needing surgery, malnutrition, choking, and concern that it signals disordered eating.
deepLead:
The cotton ball diet is a fad diet in which people swallow cotton balls, sometimes dipped in juice or smoothies, to feel full without eating food. 
It was covered by news outlets in November 2013 and has been widely condemned by health professionals as dangerous, because cotton cannot be digested and may form blockages.

name: Master Cleanse / juice cleanse

angle.text: Users do the Master Cleanse or juice cleanses for one to seven days to de-bloat and drop weight quickly. Medical sources report temporary weight loss and no evidence for the detox claims.

summary: Lemon-syrup or juice-only fasts used for quick de-bloating; medical sources report no evidence for detox claims and temporary weight loss.
note: Electrolyte imbalance and nutrient deficiency are listed risks of prolonged use.
currentQuick:
A cleanse means living on a restrictive liquid diet for days, either the Master Cleanse (lemon, maple syrup, cayenne) or fruit and vegetable juices.
Promoters say it detoxifies and slims; dietitians and health bodies report no evidence of detoxification and note that lost weight is usually regained.
How it works: Calorie and nutrient intake is cut sharply; some versions add a salt-water laxative drink. Quick scale drops generally reflect fluid, gut contents and stored glycogen rather than fat, according to general nutrition sources.
Risks and caveats: Listed risks include electrolyte disturbance, low blood sugar events in people with diabetes, dizziness, diarrhea, protein or calcium deficiency, muscle loss and rebound weight. Prolonged use of the Master Cleanse has been linked in theory to metabolic acidosis.
deepLead:
The Master Cleanse, also called the lemonade diet, is a modified juice fast in which followers consume no solid food and instead drink a mixture of lemon juice, maple syrup and cayenne pepper in water, along with tea and a daily salt-water drink. It was marketed by Stanley Burroughs from the 1940s and revived by his 1976 book The Master Cleanser. Juice cleanses more broadly restrict a person to fruit and vegetable juices for a period of usually one to seven days.
Proponents describe such cleanses as a way to remove toxins, reset the body and lose weight quickly, and in appearance communities they are sometimes used to reduce bloating or look leaner before a event or a diet phase. Dietitians and health organisations report that the detoxification claims are unsupported by scientific evidence and that any weight lost is typically regained.

name: Dehydration cuts / water cutting

chain: Drier, more defined look for a day
angle.text: Borrowed from combat sports, water cutting is used by physique-focused users to look drier and more defined for photos or events. The look is visible within hours and fades on rehydration, and the practice is not studied as a looksmaxxing method.

summary: Sweating and fluid manipulation to look drier; borrowed from combat sports, where extreme cuts have contributed to deaths.
note: Deaths have been reported in athletes after extreme dehydration cuts.
currentQuick:
Water cutting means deliberately losing body water, via sweating or fluid manipulation, to weigh less or look leaner temporarily.
It comes from combat sports and rowing; looksmaxxing and physique circles borrow it for a drier look.
How it works: Fluid is removed from the body over hours to days, often with sauna or sweat-suit use and changes in water intake, then regained afterwards.
Risks and caveats: Combat-sports deaths in 2015 to 2017 followed extreme cuts, and regulators and physicians describe acute water loss as very dangerous. Nutrition experts generally advise against it.
deepLead:
Water cutting, or dehydration cutting, is the practice of losing body water over hours or days, typically by water manipulation, sweating, sweat suits or saunas, to weigh less or look leaner. It originates in weight-class sports such as combat sports and rowing, where athletes cut rapidly to make a weight limit. In looksmaxxing and physique communities the same idea is applied to look more defined for photos or events.
Sports organisations and emergency physicians have documented serious harm from extreme cuts, including several deaths of combat-sports athletes between 2015 and 2017. Nutrition experts rarely advise on how to do it safely and generally recommend against it.

name: Zone 2 cardio

angle.text: Users do conversational-pace cardio as a low-stress way to burn calories and support fat loss without cutting into training recovery. It is popular in fitness and longevity circles, and zone-specific research for appearance goals is limited.

summary: Easy, steady cardio at conversational pace; popular, but little zone-specific research for appearance goals.
note: Sources reviewed contain no trials of Zone 2 as such.
currentQuick:
Zone 2 is steady, easy-to-moderate cardio, usually measured by heart rate or the ability to talk.
It is widely promoted for fat use and endurance, but the sources reviewed do not include trials of Zone 2 as a named method.
How it works: Low intensity relies mostly on fat for fuel, with more glycogen used as intensity rises.
Risks and caveats: General aerobic exercise is considered low-risk; people with health conditions are generally advised to consult a clinician.
deepLead:
Zone 2 cardio refers to low-to-moderate intensity steady aerobic exercise, in popular heart-rate-zone schemes the second zone, often described as a pace at which conversation remains possible. It has become popular in fitness and longevity communities and is discussed in looksmaxxing circles as a low-stress way to burn fat.
Encyclopedic sources describe aerobic exercise as repeated light-to-moderate activity over extended periods, with fat and glycogen as the main fuels and relatively more fat used at lower intensity. The Zone 2 label itself is not defined in the sources reviewed, and no published trials were reviewed on it.

name: HIIT

angle.text: HIIT is promoted as a time-efficient way to lose fat and build conditioning for a leaner physique. It is well supported for fitness, and trials show fat-loss effects modest and similar to steady cardio.

summary: Short all-out interval workouts; well supported for fitness, with modest fat-loss effects similar to steady cardio.
note: Check with a doctor first if you have heart disease, per ACSM.
currentQuick:
HIIT is exercise in hard bursts separated by short recoveries, usually finishing within half an hour.
Research shows clear gains in fitness and metabolic markers; fat-loss effects are modest.
How it works: Near-maximal efforts drive adaptations such as greater aerobic capacity, similar to those from longer moderate training.
Risks and caveats: Injury, soreness and fatigue are reported; sustained overload may disturb hormones and sleep, and people with heart conditions are advised to seek medical clearance.
deepLead:
High-intensity interval training (HIIT) alternates short, near-maximal bursts of exercise with brief recovery periods, usually in sessions under 30 minutes. A related form, sprint interval training, uses all-out efforts. It is promoted in fitness and looksmaxxing circles as a time-efficient way to lose fat and improve conditioning.
Meta-analyses find that HIIT improves cardiorespiratory fitness and several cardiometabolic markers, with body-composition changes that are modest and generally similar to moderate continuous training when compared in overweight adults.

name: 10k steps / NEAT

angle.text: Users raise daily steps and everyday activity (NEAT) as an easy way to widen a calorie deficit and lean out. The health benefits of walking are well supported, and fat-loss effects vary between people.

summary: Raising daily steps and everyday movement; benefits are well supported for health, with fat-loss effects varying by person.
note: The 10,000 figure is not an evidence-derived threshold; reviews suggest benefit near 7,000.
currentQuick:
This is about moving more through the day, measured by steps or by the energy used in non-exercise activity.
The 10,000-step goal came from 1960s Japanese pedometer marketing; newer research points to benefits at lower counts.
How it works: Everyday movement adds energy expenditure outside workouts, and the amount varies widely between individuals.
Risks and caveats: Generally low-risk; critics note the target may be unachievable for older adults or people with mobility problems.
deepLead:
The 10,000-steps-a-day target and non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT) both concern raising everyday movement rather than formal exercise. NEAT is the energy used for activities outside structured exercise, such as standing, walking, chores and fidgeting. Looksmaxxing communities discuss raising daily steps as a way to support fat loss.
The 10,000-step target is traced to 1960s Japan; a 2025 Lancet Public Health review suggested most benefit may occur around 7,000 steps per day.

name: 12-3-30 incline walking

angle.text: The viral 12% incline, 3 mph, 30 minute walk is used as a low-impact fat-loss routine for a leaner physique. Evidence is limited to one small exploratory study.

summary: Viral 12% incline, 3 mph, 30 minute treadmill walk; only one small exploratory study exists.
note: Little published research on fat-loss outcomes.
currentQuick:
A treadmill routine: 12 percent incline, 3 mph, 30 minutes.
It went viral on social media; one exploratory 2025 study has examined its metabolic responses.
How it works: Walking on a steep incline raises the effort of walking without the impact of running.
Risks and caveats: Generally considered low-risk; steep inclines can strain calves or ankles for some people.
deepLead:
The 12-3-30 workout is a treadmill routine named for its settings: a 12 percent incline, a speed of 3 miles per hour and 30 minutes of walking. It spread through social media and is discussed in looksmaxxing and fitness circles as a low-impact fat-loss routine.
Published research is very limited: a 2025 exploratory study in the International Journal of Exercise Science compared the metabolic responses of the 12-3-30 workout with self-paced treadmill running.

name: Rucking

angle.text: Users walk with a weighted backpack as low-impact cardio that burns more than plain walking and loads the back, legs and posture muscles. It is popular in fitness circles, and appearance-specific trials have not been done.

summary: Walking with a loaded backpack; popular as low-impact cardio, with no appearance-specific trials behind it.
note: Leg injuries are common in military loaded marching; civilian benefit claims are untested in the sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
Rucking means walking or hiking with a weighted backpack. It comes from military loaded marches and has been repackaged as a fitness trend.
People take it up as a lower-impact alternative to running for conditioning and calorie burn. Claims about its effects mostly rest on general exercise-physiology reasoning rather than trials of rucking itself.
How it works: The added load raises the energy cost of walking and the demand on legs, trunk and posture muscles. Proponents say the load also adds bone-loading stress.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia reports leg injuries and heat exhaustion in military loaded marching. For civilians, the sources reviewed describe starting with a light load and short sessions; no clinical trials were found.
deepLead:
Rucking is the practice of walking or hiking while carrying a weighted backpack (a rucksack) as a form of exercise. The term comes from military usage, where a "ruck march" or loaded march is a fast march over distance carrying kit; the civilian fitness version has been promoted as a low-impact way to raise the effort of walking.
Proponents describe rucking as a way to build cardiovascular fitness, muscular endurance and bone-loading stress without running, and some say it raises calorie burn well above unweighted walking. In looksmaxxing and physique circles it is discussed mainly as a body-composition and posture tool, an alternative to jogging for fat loss.
The Wikipedia article on the topic covers the military loaded march and reports no specific civilian health findings. The Grokipedia entry, which is AI-generated, makes the fitness claims but its figures should be treated cautiously. No clinical trials of civilian rucking for appearance outcomes were located.

name: Fasted cardio

chain: More energy drawn from body fat
angle.text: Fasted morning cardio is a staple of bodybuilding-style cutting, where practitioners believe low carbohydrate stores shift energy use toward body fat. Direct research on it is limited.

summary: Morning cardio before eating, a bodybuilding cutting habit with little direct research in the sources reviewed.
note: No controlled comparison of fasted and fed cardio was found in the sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
Fasted cardio means doing aerobic exercise before the day's first meal. It is common in bodybuilding cuts.
The sources reviewed contain no controlled trial comparing it with fed cardio, so claims about added fat loss are untested here.
How it works: Proponents say low carbohydrate availability after an overnight fast shifts fuel use toward fat during the session.
Risks and caveats: No harms were documented in the sources reviewed. The one related paper is a case report on bodybuilders whose routines also included heavy anabolic steroid use.
deepLead:
Fasted cardio is aerobic exercise performed after an overnight fast, typically first thing in the morning before eating. It is a staple of bodybuilding-style cutting phases, where practitioners believe that exercising with low carbohydrate stores increases the share of energy drawn from body fat.
The practice is discussed in physique and looksmaxxing circles as a way to lean out for a defined look. The sources available for this entry are thin: no trial of fasted versus fed cardio was reviewed, and the only published material in the research set is a case report of bodybuilders' contest-preparation habits.

name: Sauna / sweat suits

angle.text: Users sweat in saunas or sweat suits to drop water weight and look leaner for a day, and some believe the sweating burns fat. The weight change is visible on the scale and returns with rehydration, and direct fat-loss research is limited.

summary: Sweating in heat-trapping gear or a sauna: it moves water weight temporarily and has little direct fat-loss research.
note: Rapid fluid loss is associated with dehydration and heat strain; sources reviewed give limited detail.
currentQuick:
Sauna suits and saunas make people sweat heavily, and they are used for quick scale-weight drops, especially before weigh-ins in combat sports.
Studies in the research set looked at heat strain, energy expenditure and heat adaptation rather than lasting fat loss.
How it works: The garment or room limits heat loss, raising body temperature and sweat output. Weight lost this way is fluid.
Risks and caveats: Heat strain and dehydration are the general concerns of heat exposure; the abstracts reviewed gave little detail on adverse outcomes.
deepLead:
Sauna suits are non-breathable garments, and saunas are heated rooms, used while exercising or resting to provoke heavy sweating. Practitioners use them for temporary weight loss and in some circles believe the sweating burns fat or flushes it out; the weight lost is mostly water, which returns with rehydration.
In sport, deliberate sweating is a recognized method of rapid weight loss before weigh-ins, and a 2022 survey of elite judo athletes described such rapid loss followed by rapid regain as a regular pre-competition routine in combat sports and weightlifting. Controlled laboratory work on sauna suits has measured their effects on body temperature, sweat and energy expenditure during exercise.

name: Spot reduction exercises

angle.text: Users do ab routines and face or jaw exercises to slim a specific area. Studies cited by reference works find that fat is lost across the body rather than locally, so the local-slimming idea remains a belief.

summary: Ab or face exercises meant to burn local fat; studies reported by reference works find fat loss is systemic.
note: Mainstream sources report no significant localized fat loss; a small 2023 trial is the reported exception.
currentQuick:
Spot reduction is the idea that exercising one area, like the abs or the face, burns fat in that area. It is promoted in fitness media and looksmaxxing spaces.
Wikipedia calls it pseudoscience, and Grokipedia reports a 2022 meta-analysis of 13 studies with no significant local fat loss. Muscle building in an area can change its look.
How it works: Proponents think working a muscle draws on nearby fat. Researchers cited say fat is mobilised from the whole body according to overall energy balance, genetics and hormones.
Risks and caveats: Little direct harm is documented; the cited concern is misleading marketing, including ab-belt claims the FTC has challenged and EMS devices not FDA-cleared for fat loss.
deepLead:
Spot reduction is the belief that exercising a particular body area, such as crunches for the abdomen or facial exercises for the cheeks, preferentially burns fat stored over that area. It is widely marketed in fitness media, and in looksmaxxing communities it appears as ab routines and face or jaw exercises aimed at a leaner look.
Wikipedia describes the claim as pseudoscientific and states that the consensus among physiologists and fitness professionals is that fat loss occurs across the body with diet and exercise. Grokipedia reports that a 2022 meta-analysis of 13 studies found no significant localized fat reduction, while noting a small 2023 trial that suggested a possible exception.

name: Bulk and cut / body recomposition

angle.text: Borrowed from bodybuilding, users alternate calorie surplus and deficit phases, or attempt slow recomposition, to add muscle and then reveal it. The approach has little direct trial evidence in the sources reviewed.

summary: Cycling calorie surplus and deficit phases to add muscle and then lean out; borrowed from bodybuilding, little direct trial evidence in the sources.
note: Bulking adds some fat; muscle retention during cuts is described as uncertain.
currentQuick:
Bulking means eating in a surplus to gain muscle, cutting means eating in a deficit to lose fat, and recomposition tries to do both at once. The cycle comes from bodybuilding.
On forums people debate cycle lengths and whether to recomp instead.
How it works: Calorie surplus supplies energy for muscle growth with resistance training, and a deficit draws down fat; larger surpluses add more fat and larger deficits risk muscle loss.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia reports that some fat gain is expected in bulks and that a large deficit raises muscle loss risk. Forum discussions of drug adjuncts are untested in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Bulking and cutting is a cyclical approach to physique change: a bulk is a period of eating in a calorie surplus to gain muscle, and a cut is a period in a deficit to lose fat while keeping as much muscle as possible. Body recomposition is the alternative of trying to lose fat and gain muscle at the same time.
The approach comes from bodybuilding, where most competitors build muscle through an off-season and begin cutting about 12-14 weeks before a contest. In looksmaxxing communities it is debated: some advocate bulking to add size, others advocate recomposition to avoid fat gain, and some members discuss drug adjuncts. The sources reviewed contain no controlled trials of the strategies themselves.

name: Macro tracking apps

angle.text: Users log meals in apps such as MyFitnessPal to hit calorie and protein targets while cutting or bulking. Tracking is popular in physique circles, and self-reported intake carries accuracy limits.

summary: Food-logging apps like MyFitnessPal for hitting calorie and protein targets; popular, with self-report accuracy limits.
note: Self-reported logging has documented under-reporting; 2018 MyFitnessPal breach exposed about 150 million accounts.
currentQuick:
Macro tracking apps record what you eat against calorie and protein, carb and fat goals. MyFitnessPal is the best-known.
They are used to run bulks and cuts with numbers instead of guesses.
How it works: Users search a food database or scan barcodes and compare daily totals with targets the app estimates or the user sets.
Risks and caveats: Reference sources cite logging inaccuracy (under-reporting and unreliable restaurant entries) and a 2018 data breach at MyFitnessPal. Other harms were not covered in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Macro tracking apps let users log food and drink against daily calorie and macronutrient (protein, carbohydrate, fat) targets. The best-known example is MyFitnessPal, which describes itself as an app and website for looking up the nutritional content of foods, logging intake against goals, building meal plans and tracking exercise.
In physique and looksmaxxing communities, logging is used to manage bulking and cutting phases and protein targets. Research on tracking is not covered by the sources used for this entry, so its effect on body composition is not described here.
